stories.summary: The author argues that despite impressive headlines like LLMs solving Navier-Stokes equations, they remain fundamentally limited as autonomous workers because most real-world tasks lack the rigorous formal specifications necessary to prevent reward hacking and errors. The core bottleneck is that creating precise specifications requires expensive domain experts and rigorous validation, which doesn't scale to the volume of output LLMs can produce, and human review—the alternative—is slow, expensive, and itself vulnerable to manipulation. Consequently, LLMs will mostly function as "cracked interns" useful only in specific niches: cheap labor replacements, narrowly-defined repetitive tasks, or specialized fields like chip design where validation failures are critical enough to justify the specification costs.

jobs.text: We're the system of record for the Canadian vehicle: raw automotive data turned into facts that can be checked. Our open-source VIN decoder sits underneath a government vehicle registry. Some of what's interesting: - A government registry, a manufacturer's own filing, a listing site and an insurance record will describe the same truck four different ways, and nothing in any of those files says they're the same truck. Reconciling that, for every vehicle in the country, in a way that holds up when a regulator asks how you know, is most of the data work. - Seventeen characters on a door frame encode manufacturer, plant, model year and build attributes — badly, inconsistently, and differently per manufacturer. Public reference data covers some of it. The rest gets worked out from filings, recall documents, and patterns inferred across millions of vehicles. - We read vehicles directly over OBD-II now. Forty modules answered on a recent Hyundai, each reporting its own part number and installed software version. Nothing downstream of the VIN moves when a module is reflashed, so no registration, history report or dealer system knows what software is actually in a car. Hiring: VIN Decode Engineer, Data Platform Engineer, Infrastructure Engineer, Founding Engineer (dealer platform). TypeScript, Postgres, Cloudflare Workers. Full descriptions and apply: https://cardog.app/careers

stackOverflowQuestions.title: How can bounded-contexts interact with each other in DDD?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: So, imagine an app with two entities, for example, Order and Product . Both have their own lifecycle, so they are essentially bounded contexts. Let's say in code it would look like order/{domain, application, infra, …} and product/{domain, application, infra, …} . On the infra layer we work with, for example, a relational DB, and here it's easy. There are tables orders , products , and order_products , because it's many-to-many. We just organize it through PK/FK relations. But the problem starts showing itself in the code. For example, we go to the repo and call this.ordersRepo.findOne() . Inside, it can fetch literally everything: products, orders, etc., BUT it has to return an Order entity, which is described in the domain layer. This is where the problem begins, and it consists in the fact that Order, according to DDD, should NOT know about Product, etc. It encapsulates its own invariants, but in no way should it contain a field like products: Product[] or productIds: ProductId[] . So now the question is: how to work with this at all? Like, if we follow this, it becomes impossible to even create an order. For example, some this.orderFactory.create(…) , even though it returns an Order, can't be persisted, because it has no information about the products. It's also impossible to work with business logic that involves two domains, for example, that an order can't contain more than 4 products or something like that.

stackOverflowQuestions.title: Redmine CSV export writes a bare parent id that the importer reads as a row index, so re-importing flattens the hierarchy
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I maintain a work breakdown structure in Redmine and edit it in bulk by exporting the issues to CSV, changing them in a spreadsheet, and importing the file back through the built-in importer. Subjects, dates, versions and custom fields all survive that round-trip. The parent/child structure does not. Every re-imported issue is created as a root issue, and the tree I started with is gone. What makes it easy to miss is that the import reports success: there is no warning and no failed row, so I only notice when the Gantt chart comes back as a flat list. The Redmine wiki page "HowTo import issues" documents two forms for the parent column. A value with a leading hash sign refers to an issue that already exists, by its id. A plain number refers instead to the position of a row inside the file being imported, counting data rows only. That second rule seems to be what breaks the round-trip, because the export writes plain numbers. An issue whose parent is issue 1176 is exported with 1176 in the parent column and no hash sign. On the way back in, the importer does not look for issue 1176; it looks for the 1176th row of the file. My file has a few hundred rows, that position does not exist, and the reference resolves to nothing. The same value means one thing on the way out and something else on the way in. To check whether the two forms really behave differently I imported a small file of four rows. The leading column was left unmapped on the mapping screen, since ids are assigned by Redmine: #,Project,Tracker,Parent task,Subject,Status,Priority,Start date,Due date T1,MYPROJECT,Task,#1176,ZZ_TEST_AP_Domain,New,Normal,2026/10/15,2027/03/31 T2,MYPROJECT,Task,1,ZZ_TEST_BLK_A,New,Normal,2026/10/15,2027/03/31 T3,MYPROJECT,Task,1,ZZ_TEST_BLK_B,New,Normal,2026/10/15,2027/03/31 T4,MYPROJECT,Task,2,ZZ_TEST_SUB_OF_A,New,Normal,2026/10/15,2027/03/31 Row 1 points at an existing issue with the hash form.
